California races
The editorial board recommends
Governor: Xavier Becerra Democrat Voting rights attorney
Why we're endorsing
The entire purpose of electing an experienced politician like Becerra is to feel confident that he will have the discernment to know which big ideas to go after and which to pass on, that he will arrive on the job with a meaningful, achievable agenda and actionable plans, and that he can communicate that agenda transparently and effectively to the public. We do not feel confident. All that said, Becerra’s Republican opponent, Steve Hilton — an ally of President Donald Trump — is no viable option.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-governor-race-22494871.php)
Lieutenant Governor: Fiona Ma Democrat State treasurer/CPA
Why we're endorsing
Fiona Ma comes with significant baggage — which is why she wasn’t our first choice for the role in the June primary. But she has the competence and experience to smoothly assume the duties of the state’s No. 2 office. Given the ramblings of her opponent, we cautiously recommend Ma for lieutenant governor.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/lieutenant-governor-california-state-election-22404751.php)
Secretary of State: Shirley Weber Democrat California secretary of state ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
California is no ocean of calm when it comes to elections. The need for steady and trustworthy leadership from our secretary of state cannot be understated. Shirley Weber’s breadth of experience, willingness to do the right thing and fierce advocacy for voting rights make her the strongest candidate.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/shirley-weber-secretary-state-california-22228493.php)
Controller: Malia Cohen Democrat State controller ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
The State Controller’s Office is California’s internal auditor — empowered to investigate how state agencies and local governments are spending state funds. Overall, we think Cohen has made enough progress to merit another term. But Californians should stay watchful to ensure she keeps the positive momentum going.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/malia-cohen-state-controller-california-22242981.php)
Treasurer: Eleni Kounalakis Democrat Lieutenant governor
Why we're endorsing
The California state treasurer is the main banker, financier and asset manager for the world’s fourth-largest economy. With her thorough grasp of the treasurer’s complex duties and the political gravitas to get things done, Eleni Kounalakis deserves your vote.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-eleni-kounalakis-california-treasurer-22154455.php)
Attorney General: Rob Bonta Democrat Attorney general ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
In our endorsement interview, incumbent Rob Bonta’s calm, clear and concise grasp of the complexities and nuances of California law — honed through more than eight years in the state Assembly — surpassed that of most of the current gubernatorial candidates.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/rob-bonta-attorney-general-california-22194540.php)
Insurance Commissioner: Ben Allen Democrat State senator
Why we're endorsing
The insurance market has began to show signs of recovery. Insurers are finally starting to write new policies in the state. Electing a rash insurance commissioner could reverse that progress and cause the market to implode. Ben Allen has what it takes to hold insurers accountable and regulate their market conduct while also fostering the conditions necessary to keep the market stable.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/insurance-commissioner-california-allen-kim-22321376.php)
Superintendent of Public Instruction: Richard Barrera School board member
Why we're endorsing
Richard Barrera is an increasingly rare California progressive who brings all parties to the table, a skill that the new state superintendent of public instruction will need as the role of the office changes.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/superintendent-richard-barrera-sonja-shaw-22376416.php)
State Board of Equalization District 1: It's complicated
Why we're endorsing
The Chronicle Editorial Board writes that the Board of Equalization shouldn’t exist.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/john-pimentel-board-equalization-california-22204357.php)
State Board of Equalization District 2: It's complicated
Why we're endorsing
The Chronicle Editorial Board writes that the Board of Equalization shouldn’t exist.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/john-pimentel-board-equalization-california-22204357.php)
California propositions
The editorial board recommends
Proposition 1: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Befitting the broad consensus on California’s affordability crisis, Prop 1 has no formal opposition. The measure is the product of years of legislative sausage-making and is unwieldy. But the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait — and Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop1-california-housing-vote-22442444.php)
Proposition 2: Yes
Why we're endorsing
If used to the fullest extent, Prop 2 could improve California’s budget stability, permitting the state to cover about 50% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years. Voters should pass Prop 2 and hold lawmakers accountable to their promise to be more responsible stewards of taxpayer money.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-2-money-california-22468892.php)
Proposition 3: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but also keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php)
Proposition 4: No
Why we're endorsing
All available research indicates that the effectiveness of a public campaign finance program depends on how it’s designed. Prop 4 has a fatal flaw that opens the door to limited taxpayer funds being wasted on efforts that don’t meaningfully move the needle — at a time of widespread budget deficits.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php)
Proposition 5: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials. The process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-5-recall-california-22458510.php)
Proposition 37: Yes
Why we're endorsing
Prop 37 promises to make it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership. Its scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change the state’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php)
Proposition 38: No
Why we're endorsing
Wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world? Prop 38 positions itself as such a balm. In fact, it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years. It would give billions to an institute co-founded by billionaire Michael Milken, also known as the “junk bond king,” who was pardoned by Trump in 2020.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Proposition 39: No
Why we're endorsing
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. But even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California, Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-proposition-39-voter-fraud-california-22463918.php)
Proposition 40: No
Why we're endorsing
Ultimately, neither this editorial board nor anyone else has any idea what the full effect of Prop 40 will be. Even Emmanuel Saez, the French economist and an author of Prop 40, has conceded that his measure is an “experiment.” If it backfires, California will have chased away its cash cows with no backup plan. No one is coming to save us, and it won’t be the wealthy who suffer. California isn’t a lab rat. Voters shouldn’t allow our state to be treated like one.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
Proposition 41: No
Why we're endorsing
Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund. But really it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)
Proposition 42: No
Why we're endorsing
Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what the backers of this measure would have you believe. In reality, it’s just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax. You don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php)
Proposition 43: No endorsement
Why we're endorsing
Despite commanding far less attention than the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a question reverberating throughout the nation: Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work? We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements California’s broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)
Proposition 44: No
Why we're endorsing
On its surface, everything about Prop 44 on California’s November ballot looks appealing. But it creates a complex administrative and legal regime that will drain limited staff time and resources from nonprofit clinics while distracting from patient care.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php)
Proposition 45: No
Why we're endorsing
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, and some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45. But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22468905.php)
Advertisement
U.S. Congress
The editorial board recommends
U.S. House District 11: Scott Wiener Democrat State senator
Why we're endorsing
With Scott Wiener, San Franciscans would send the state’s most relentless and effective legislator to Washington to zero in on universal healthcare, humane immigration policies, protections for the LGBTQ community and preserving democracy from President Donald Trump. Connie Chan, meanwhile, has a policy agenda and legislative track record that’s as spotty as it is sparse.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
U.S. House District 14: Aisha Wahab Democrat Member of Congress ▪ Incumbent
Why we're endorsing
Congress in the age of Trump is no place to learn on the job. Wahab is the only candidate prepared for the gravity of the moment.
Read the full editorial (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/aisha-wahab-district-14-california-22268931.php)
California Supreme Court
The editorial board recommends
Kelli M. Evans: Yes
Why we're endorsing
California has a thoughtful and thorough system in place for appointing judges. Every four years, voters are given the important yet perplexing job of deciding whether to retain a slate of judges who already serve. None of the justices up for retention in the November election have been cited for disciplinary matters on the Commission on Judicial Performance’s database, nor have our queries into their backgrounds turned up any red flags. We recommend a “yes” vote on all of them.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 37
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 37: the California Middle- Class Homeownership & Family Home Construction Act. Proposition 37 creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction-with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
California has the second-worst homeownership rate in the nation; rising costs push homeownership further out of reach every year.
With the statewide median home price now exceeding $930,000, a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000 just to get in the door. Teachers, nurses, veterans, and firefighters work hard and pay their bills. They can afford monthly mortgage payments but are locked out of homeownership in the communities where they live and work because down payment requirements are too high.
Proposition 37 gives working and middle-class Californians a fair shot at homeownership.
KEEPING HOMEOWNERSHIP WITHIN REACH.
Prop. 37 is a practical solution. It makes consumer-friendly, low-interest downpayment assistance loans available to qualified California residents for purchasing a newly built home, with no cost to taxpayers.
This is not a handout. Homebuyers must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans.
Prop. 37 is designed for renters, first-time homebuyers, and working families who earn too much to qualify for renter assistance programs, but not enough to save the massive down payment required to buy a home.
“Proposition 37 will boost homeownership without burdening taxpayers. As a state revenue bond, downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers.” -Malia Cohen, California State Controller
BUILDS MORE HOMES, CREATES GOOD JOBS.
California hasn’t built enough homes to keep up with demand. By helping qualified buyers purchase newly built homes, Prop. 37 will help accelerate construction, creating thousands of good-paying jobs and generating economic investment.
Expanding the housing supply helps workers and families to stay in California, build equity, raise their children, and live in the communities where they work.
ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
Taxpayer advocates and California’s Legislative Analyst agree: Proposition 37 has no cost to taxpayers. Loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers-not taxpayers.
STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND CONSUMER PROTECTIONS.
Prop. 37 includes fiscal accountability and transparency requirements, construction accountability standards, and annual audits detailing the status of loans made and the fund’s financial condition.
Consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans, protections from unfair lending practices, strict limits on lender fees, and no penalty for early repayment.
BROAD, BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats & Republicans, labor and businesses, construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers Association, and United Nurses Association of California.
For generations, homeownership provided stability, security, and a path to the middle class. But today, that path is simply out of reach for too many Californians. Proposition 37 is a practical solution that tackles one of the biggest barriers to homeownership, without burdening taxpayers.
Vote YES to expand middle-class homeownership, build more homes, create good jobs, and give working Californians a fair chance to live, work, raise a family, and stay in California.
VoteYeson37.com
Danny Curtin , Director
California Conference of Carpenters
Fiona Ma , Boardmember
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA)
David West , Chair
California State Commanders Veterans Council

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

Prop
37
CA
Prop
37
|
Bond
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
Authorizes $25 billion in state revenue bonds to encourage the construction of new homes and increase middle-class homeownership through second mortgages.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR supports the creation of new tools and financing to promote homeownership, and these revenue bonds would have no impact on the state’s General Fund. The focus on new construction will increase the supply of for-sale homes in the state and allow homebuyers to build generational wealth through home equity. While Prop. 37 could have focused more specifically on supporting populations that face barriers to homeownership, we believe its contribution to overall homeownership rates makes it worthy of support.
Vote YES
What Prop. 37 Would Do
Proposition 37 would authorize revenue bonds for fixed-rate second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, helping them afford a 20% down payment. Home loan borrowers would have to repay the bonds and administrative costs. The California Housing Finance Agency would offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a newly constructed home. The bonds could not be used for existing homes. 1 Other requirements:
Homebuyers would have to make a minimum 3% down payment.
Second-mortgage loans would be limited to 17% of a home’s purchase price.
Homebuyers would put down 20% equity at purchase to eliminate the need for private mortgage insurance.
The maximum sales price for a qualified new home could not exceed 125% of the Federal Housing Finance Agency conforming loan limit for that county. (For example, the 2026 limit for San Francisco is $1,249,125; 125% of that limit would be $1,561,406).
Homebuyers would have to be California residents for at least one year and would agree to occupy the home as a primary residence.
Family income could not exceed 200% of the area median income (AMI) in the county or metropolitan statistical area where the new home is located.
The Backstory
The cost of housing in California has made homeownership increasingly challenging for many households, especially for Black and Latinx families who have experienced housing discrimination and have less inherited wealth, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. 2
This second-mortgage program would be available to households earning up to 200% of AMI, or $401,600 for a family of four in San Francisco.
Homeownership assistance has been a priority for former State Senator Bob Hertzberg. In 2022, he attempted to get a measure similar to Prop. 37 on the ballot through the state Legislature, but it failed. Former State Senator Anthony Portantino picked up the effort after Hertzberg was termed out of office, but he couldn't move legislation either. Hertzberg, now a private citizen, pivoted to a signature-gathering campaign and submitted more than 900,000 signatures this year to qualify Prop. 37 for the ballot. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
The racial equity impacts of Prop. 37 are unclear. While the Bay Area Equity Atlas found that the overall homeownership rate in the Bay Area is lower for Black (37%), Latinx (42%), and Native American (42%) households, this measure’s high cap of households earning up to 200% of AMI may disproportionately benefit Asian and white households, who have higher incomes and can more easily afford homeownership. In the Bay Area, the median income of Black and Latinx households is below 80% of AMI, according to U.S. Census data.
Pros
Prop. 37 would potentially create more homeownership opportunities in a state that, at 55.8%, has one of the lowest homeownership rates in the nation.
The measure focuses on new construction to increase housing supply rather than increasing demand for existing housing stock.
It would require the California Housing Finance Agency to conduct an independent annual audit of the program to ensure that bond proceeds are used in a manner consistent with the requirements.
Cons
Prop. 37 is not limited to first-time homebuyers and may therefore benefit Californians who could enter the market without its support.
The program is not targeted to low- or moderate-income households, allowing households with earnings of up to 200% of AMI to qualify. The maximum sales price may go up to 125% of the Federal Housing Finance Agency conforming loan limit.
Vote YES

## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

###### Abstract
Strategic voting is a canonical failure mode for collective choice: a voter may obtain a more preferred outcome by reporting a ballot that differs from its true preferences.
This paper introduces an oracle-based benchmark for testing whether large language model (LLM) voters can discover and execute such manipulations.
Each instance gives an LLM voter a true preference ranking, the other voters’ ballots, a deterministic voting rule, and a prompt condition.
An exact oracle enumerates every feasible report by the LLM voter, computes the sincere outcome, identifies all profitable reports, and records the best achievable outcome.
The benchmark therefore supplies ground truth for strategic success without human labels or subjective grading of explanations.
The benchmark covers plurality, Borda, approval, instant-runoff voting, and Copeland-style pairwise majority voting; prompt conditions separate sincere, strategic, civic, and expert framings.

# Do your own research!
## Abstract
Philosophical tradition and conspiracy theorists converge in suggesting that ordinary people ought to do their own research, rather than accept the word of others.
In this paper, I argue that it’s no accident that conspiracy theorists value lay research on expert topics: such research is likely to undermine knowledge, via its effects on truth and justification.
Accepting expert testimony is a far more reliable route to truth.
Nevertheless, lay research has a range of benefits; in particular, it is likely to lead to greater understanding, even when it does not lead to knowledge.
I argue that we can reap most of the genuine benefits of lay research while minimizing the risks by engaging in exploratory, rather than truth-directed, inquiry.
...
On topics on which there is a large body of truly expert knowledge, and in which there are official stories (or a range of official stories: a range, that is, of genuinely expert views), doing one’s own research is epistemically risky.
...
## The value of engagement
We often and predictably do much better *with regard to knowledge* by relying on testimony, rather than by doing our own research.
The former is routinely more reliable than the latter; doing our own research risks the truth of our beliefs and their justification (Matheson, 2022).
...
If all this is true, then laypeople regularly do better to defer to testimony than to inquire for themselves, at least so far as the aim is acquiring knowledge.
